en: The *Sūtra on the Mother of Demons* Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator is lost, now appended to the Western Jin Record.
When the Buddha traveled to the country of Daudou, there was at that time a woman in the kingdom who had many children and whose nature was extremely wicked.
There was one who constantly delighted in stealing and would kill and eat the children of others.
The families whose children had vanished did not know who had taken them, and they wandered through the streets and alleys wailing.
People returned from their errands and discussed the matter together; this continued for more than a day.
Ānanda and the assembly of śramaṇas went out and repeatedly encountered people weeping; upon returning, they discussed together their grief for the family that had lost its son.
The Buddha, knowing the discussion among the śramaṇas, went to where the assembly of śramaṇas was.
The Buddha asked the assembly of śramaṇas:
"What were you discussing just now?
The śramaṇas and Ānanda replied to the Buddha, saying:
"Previously, while going out for alms, I saw many people weeping in the streets. I immediately asked those who were weeping:
'Why are you weeping?'"
They replied, "A child has died in our family; we do not know where the corpse lies.
Thus there were those wailing like this, not from one household alone, for all had lost their children.
The Buddha then spoke for Ānanda and the assembly of śramaṇas:
"The one who stole the child in this land was no ordinary person; it was the Mother of Ghosts (Hārītī) who manifested as such."
Having been born as a human in this life, he delighted in the practice of stealing others' children.
This mother had a thousand sons: five hundred sons were in the heavens, and five hundred sons were in the world.
The thousand sons were all kings of ghosts, each king followed by tens of thousands of ghosts.
Thus, five hundred ghost-kings harassed the devas in the heavens,
while another five hundred ghost-kings harassed the emperors and the people in the world.
"Even the gods can do nothing against these five hundred ghost kings.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"The Mother of Ghost Children has come and is here within this kingdom."
"Now, would it not be well to issue a decree forbidding the theft of others' children?
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"May he be made so that he no longer steals others' children.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"By what skillful means should he be made not to steal others' children again?"
The Buddha then said to Ānanda:

"Go to where that mother resides; once all the śramaṇas have together waited for her to come out, you must all gather up her son and bring him back, placing him within the vihāra to escape [the danger]."
The assembly of śramaṇas immediately went there.
Waiting for the mother to go out, they followed her and gathered up her children.
Having obtained a thousand children, they fled and hid them within the vihāra.
The mother then went out again to steal another person's child and brought it into the house; not seeing her own child, she abandoned the other's child and did not dare to kill it again.
He immediately went out to search for his son, but throughout the house, he could not find where the son was.
He then went out into the streets and alleys, but could not find him anywhere in the city.
He further went outside the city walls to search, but still could not find him; he then returned to the city and walked along the roads, weeping and wailing.
After ten days had passed in this manner, the mother went mad.

With her hair disheveled, she entered the marketplace, wailing and beating her breast, throwing herself prostrate and looking up to heaven while crying out in the dialect of Liang. She was no longer able to eat or drink.
The Buddha sent a śramaṇa to go and look at her; seeing her mother, he asked, "Why are you in the marketplace with disheveled hair, weeping?
The mother then replied to the śramaṇa:
"I weep because many of my children have perished.
The śramaṇa said,
"Do you wish to recover your children?"
The mother replied,
"I wish to obtain it. The śramaṇa said:
"If you truly desire to obtain him, there is a Buddha here whom you may go to question.
A Buddha knows the affairs of both the future and the past;
if you go to him, you will be able to recover your son."
Upon hearing these words, her mother’s mind was filled with joy and she attained liberation; she then followed the śramaṇa away.
Arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, she approached him with joy and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha then asked his mother,
"Why are you weeping in the marketplace?
The mother replied to the Buddha:
“Because my son has perished.
The Buddha asked the mother,
“Where did you leave your son so that he perished?”
The mother remained silent and said nothing.
The Buddha questioned her again:
"Where did you go after abandoning your son, that you have now returned?"
He remained silent and spoke no word.
The mother, knowing that her son was a thief who had committed evil, immediately rose and paid homage to the Buddha, prostrating herself with her head and face touching the ground:
"It is because of my own ignorance."
The Buddha asked again:
"Do you have a son whom you love?
The mother replied:
"I have a son who always wishes to sit or stand by my side.
The Buddha asked again, "You have a son; do you know how to love him?"
For what reason does the Sun go about stealing the children of others?
Others have children just as you do; when their children perish, their families likewise walk the roads wailing just as you do.
"You, on the contrary, have stolen a man's child and eaten him; after death, you shall enter the Great Mountain Hell.
Upon hearing these words, the mother was struck with terror.
The Buddha asked again:
“Would you rather have your son back?
The mother immediately rose and again placed her head upon the ground, saying,
“I pray that you will have pity on me.”
The Buddha then said to his mother,
"If your son were here, would you not be able to repent for yourself?
If you can repent for yourself, I shall restore your son to you."
The mother said,
"I am able to repent myself.
The Buddha said:
"If you are able to repent of your own accord, how should you repent?
The mother said,
"I shall listen to the Buddha’s admonitions and repent according to the Buddha’s words."
“If the Buddha returns my child to me, I shall not dare to depart from what the Buddha has spoken.
The Buddha asked, “Is it truly as you say?”
The mother said,
"I truly believe as the Buddha has spoken.
The Buddha then conferred upon her the five precepts:
First, refrain from taking life;
second, refrain from stealing;
third, refrain from sexual misconduct.
Fourth, not to engage in divisive speech;
fifth, not to drink alcohol.
When he was able to repay [his debts], he returned everything to his son.
The Buddha then spoke for him, saying:
"You have a thousand sons; I shall now declare the names of all one thousand sons.
Five hundred of your sons are in the heavens, all of whom are kings among ghosts. Leading their ghostly officials and retinues, they maliciously harm and harass the celestial beings."
His five hundred sons remain in the world, harassing the people.
Your son acts as a king of ghosts, leading tens of thousands of spirits.
Thus, these five hundred sons lead ghost officials and their retinues in numbers beyond reckoning.
Extremely jealous, malicious, and evil, some claim to be tree spirits;
some act as earth spirits;
and some act as water spirits.
Some falsely appear as brothers, wives, or children, lamenting the injustices suffered by their households and kin;
some manifest as sea deities;
and some manifest as deities of ships and carriages.
Some act as deities of dwellings;
some claim to be deities who roam in the darkness of night;
and some cause people to awaken from their dreams.
Some cause others to be terrified or act as sorcerers for others;
some claim to have died by the stars or claim to have died of disease—such troublemakers are found scattered in various places.

Extremely jealous and malicious, they falsely claim that people must offer sacrifices by slaughtering animals for them; yet people, unaware of this, slaughter many creatures for their food, thinking these are spirits—though even these spirits are unwilling to eat such things.
He is extremely jealous and malicious, desiring to cause others to commit murder and wishing to send them into hell.
He resolutely refuses to eat [the sacrificial meat].
He rejoices when he sees people performing sacrifices.
In this way, such ghosts cannot protect the lives of humans; they only increase their transgressions.
Foolish people do not realize this and remain bound by the poverty of the ghosts.

When the Mother of Ghost Children heard these words spoken by the Buddha, she immediately repented with single-minded devotion and attained the stage of Srotāpanna, thereby knowing the matters of coming and going.
Kneeling with his right knee on the ground, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I was foolish and ignorant, not realizing that my evil deeds had persisted through so many lifetimes.
Now that I have attained the observance of the precepts and contemplate the Way of the Centered Mean, my mind perceives everything clearly."
I have again seen my thousand sons.
Now I truly know that whatever the Buddha reaches for and whatever he utters comes to fulfillment.
I pray that the Buddha will have compassion for me!

I wish to dwell beside the Buddha’s vihāra; I wish to summon the King of a Thousand Sons; I wish to cause him to enter into a covenant with the Buddha; and I wish to repay the kindness of the beings of the heavens above and the world below.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent! It is very good that you have such an intention."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should recite these words and remain by the side of the Buddha’s vihāra.
When the people of that country who have no sons come seeking children, you shall grant them sons according to their own wishes."
"I shall command my children and provide attendants to protect you;
henceforth, they must not trouble you again.

Those who wish to make a petition to the Mother of Ghosts (Hārītī) should use the vessel named *Buddhamani*; her elder sister is named Zhinü, and among the spirits of heaven and earth, it is this *Buddhamani* vessel that belongs to her.
He who rules within the four seas, whose livelihood involves ships and carriages and who possesses property—all such persons belong to Maṇibhadra.
Maṇibhadra has entered into a solemn covenant with the Buddha and received the precepts; he is charged with protecting the persons and wealth of men.
To the host of the fire-heater: if there is a birth, one should provide for its rescue.
There is a Heavenly King named Vaiśravaṇa, who presides over the four worlds; he protects human life, and whenever one goes out or comes in, one should always seek his vows from Vaiśravaṇa.
There is a great ghost king named Asura, who presides over all dragon kings and poisonous vapors. When people seek his vows, he ensures that poison does not afflict them.
One should seek his vows with a compassionate heart; there is no need for thanks, nor does he devour anyone.
As for those who seek through aspiration, it depends on what each person seeks;
however, one must ultimately have nothing to seek and not hold others accountable.
When people come before the *buddhavatamsaka-maṇi* bowl, they perform a prostration.
The Sutra on the Mother of Demons Spoken by the Buddha.
